items.headline: AI trade meltdown: Nasdaq into correction as chip and neocloud names collapse
items.summary: Thursday's sell-off erased Wednesday's post-midterm rally. The S&P 500 fell about 4.4% and the Nasdaq about 5.5%, with the Nasdaq-100 posting its largest daily drop since the 2020 pandemic and the Magnificent Seven losing more than $1 trillion of market cap. Chip and data-center names led: SanDisk, Nebius, Micron, Marvell and peers plunged as traders priced slower AI infrastructure buildout. On X, @KobeissiLetter framed it as leverage meeting a sentiment flip — "fundamentally, nothing has changed" in an hour — while Nvidia briefly printed near a ~13× forward P/E, cheaper than the S&P.
items.short: Nasdaq −5.5% into correction; Mag7 −$1T; chips and neoclouds lead the wipeout.

items.author: Gavin Baker
items.text:
The governor-elect of Texas, Gina Hinojosa, has explicitly said that all currently permitted datacenters in Texas will be allowed to finish construction. This essentially covers all of the 2027 and likely well into 2028.

She is going to pass laws that ensure that all *newly* permitted datacenters going forward for delivery in 2028/2029 will pay taxes, commit to no increase in power prices for consumers, don’t impact water availability for people, be constructed with union labor and give “Texans a seat at the table.”

Sounds reasonable. She doesn’t want to lose a lot of good blue collar jobs and property taxes for small towns in rural Texas.

Datacenter commentary starts at 6:30 in this interview.

Also attaching her official campaign position from her website in the next post.

Sidenote: After watching a bunch of her speeches and interviews, I do think she is a political talent and probably has a future in national politics.

items.author: Jukan
items.text:
Today I met with a veteran investor who argued that memory stocks are not cheap even at a P/E of 3. Below is an edited version of our conversation.

Memory LTAs are basically meaningless. The best the LTAs being signed today can do is get customers to shoulder part of the memory makers' capex. Once prices fall, customers will gladly forfeit their deposits (prepayments) and walk away from the LTAs.

Historically, whenever prices fell more than 60% from the peak, customers broke their LTAs even after signing them.
So even if a 2027 shortage is certain and the stocks trade at a P/E of 3 on 2027 operating profit, 2028 operating profit is uncertain, which makes it hard to justify a higher valuation.

He went on to argue that even if 2028 operating profit were certain, we would still have to account for 2029 operating profit.

I pushed back and asked why the market doesn't discount TSMC the same way. Why does TSMC get such a high valuation? Wouldn't TSMC also take a big hit if the AI boom fades?

His answer: the problem was how violently memory prices rose in the first place.
If memory makers had raised prices in a healthy way like TSMC, it might be a different story. But because they hiked prices like a commodity, the market has no choice but to treat memory stocks like commodity stocks.

Even if memory makers stay in shortage through 2030, he said, the market will price in the risk of oversupply in 2031.

He closed his argument this way: even at 3x 2027 earnings, if memory prices fall in 2028 by enough to break LTAs, that 3x multiple on 2027 works out to 7.8 to 10x on 2028. So current valuations are not cheap.

items.headline: Musk: Cybertruck production winds down mid-2027 for Cybercab
items.summary: Elon Musk said Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to free capacity for Cybercab. The Austin plant is the only known Cybertruck assembly site; Musk did not say whether the truck moves elsewhere. Lead engineer Wes Morrill called Cybertruck a technology platform that “lives on through Cybercab.”
items.short: Cybertruck production at Giga Texas winds down mid-2027 for Cybercab ramp.

items.author: Paul Millerd
items.text:
2027 Is going to be an absolutely wild year for knowledge work 

I actually think there will be far more opportunity in terms of jobs, but you are going to have to work with agentic coding models. It's still early so a lot of stuff isn't abstracted away 

I have had a surprising amount of people reach out to me in the last 2 months, wanting to just talk with somebody who's gone through letting go of a fancy work identity

The good news is that many people get to a spot where they feel happier about work.  Does that mean a guaranteed path to always making money in a very stable and secure way? No. But it does mean there are far more ways to work in today's world and be satisfied with that 

I think the key is to not trade your present for the future. Fear and worry. And the sense that you are "behind," are always stealing your present. And the present is the only way you can actually channel curiosity or creativity - the best way to embrace an emergent path

items.title: Treat investing the same way you treat life
items.author: Paradis
items.summary: On crash days, Paradis recalls a CIO mentor’s rule: treat investing like life. Both trade certainty today for uncertainty tomorrow; both reward patience after testing it. The first rule in either domain is survival — you can recover from most losses, not from the one that takes you out of the game.

items.title: Volatility isn’t the enemy; permanent loss is
items.author: Chris Camillo
items.summary: Camillo argues Wall Street sold long-term investors on equating volatility with risk, then sold them “low-vol” products. For decade-scale wealth building, 50%+ drawdowns aren’t the real enemy — permanent capital loss is. The goal is maximizing long-term wealth without enough risk to blow yourself up, not the smoothest path.

items.title: Short payback ≠ great equity return on AI infrastructure
items.author: Rose Celine
items.summary: A careful walk through why recovering equipment cost quickly is not the same as earning an attractive return on the full economic life of AI infrastructure. Financing, timing of cash flows, replacement spend and who captures value (infra vs applications) can leave common equity with mediocre outcomes even when the physical assets “work.”

items.headline: Google commits $17B to its first Wyoming data center
items.summary: Google announced a $17 billion investment for its first Wyoming data center in Laramie County, partnering with Tallgrass, Black Hills Energy, AEP and Related Digital. Power includes a planned 702 MW Bloom Energy fuel-cell plant with carbon capture under an AEP PPA, plus air cooling to cut water use. The announcement landed the same day AI infrastructure stocks were selling off.
items.short: Google: $17B first Wyoming DC; Bloom fuel cells + CCS; air-cooled.

items.title: Four Cards
items.rule: If a card is red on one side, it has a circle on the other.
items.explanation: Red could hide something that breaks the rule; Square breaks it if the other side turns out to be Red. Circle can't break it (the rule never says only those cards have it), and Green isn't covered by the rule at all. Most people pick the card that matches the rule's second half instead of the one that could falsify it.

items.author: a16z
items.text:
For two decades, writing the exploit was the bottleneck in a cyberattack. AI made that step cheap, and patching hasn't gotten faster:

- On average, attacks went from landing 63 days after disclosure in 2018-19 to 7 days before it in 2025

- A working exploit went from a skilled person's month to a few hours of machine time

- The median time to fully fix a known-exploited bug rose to 43 days

a16z's @asaf_ez and @steph_zhang expect a long, expensive worm era, hitting hardest where systems can't update fast: hospitals, schools, small water systems. …
